newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge radio says Hun Sen blocking talks.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge radio says Hun Sen blocking talks.

text.p: Cambodia's Khmer Rouge guerrilla group said in a radio broadcast on Wednesday that Second Prime Minister Hun Sen was trying to block talks to end their war because he feared the political consequences of peace.

The radio, for years the guerrillas' main propaganda mouthpiece, said Hun Sen was afraid of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh's political alliance, the National United Front, which the guerrillas have said they want to join.

"Prince Norodom Ranariddh has sent his representatives to come to negotiate with...Khieu Samphan. The negotiations are for national forces to join together to find real national reconciliation, real peace and really finish the war," the radio said.
The clandestine radio is controlled by the guerrillas, who broke with Khmer Rouge chief Pol Pot last month and detained him at their base at Anlong Veng in northern Cambodia.

Khmer Rouge frontman Khieu Samphan is president of the guerrillas' provisional government while military commander Ta Mok remains in control of the Anlong Veng area, political analysts in Phnom Penh said.
"(Vietnamese) communists and their puppet, Hun Sen, are firmly opposed (to the talks)...the reason is they are afraid of the great forces of solidarity in the National United Front," the radio said.
The radio, which frequently attacks Hun Sen and his alleged links with Vietnam, made no mention of Pol Pot or Ta Mok.
Ranariddh and his FUNCINPEC party have been negotiating with the Khmer Rouge in Anlong Veng for some time.

But Ranariddh said last week the talks could not move forward until Khieu Samphan announced on the radio that he was formally breaking all links with Pol Pot and recognised the Cambodian constitution.
The radio has yet to broadcast any such statement.

Hun Sen, who heads a deadlocked coalition government with Ranariddh, declared the talks with the Khmer Rouge illegal. He has demanded the unconditional surrender of all Khmer Rouge leaders and ruled out any amnesty deals for any defecting leaders.

Political analysts in Phnom Penh say Cambodia's next general election in May could be very close. If Ranariddh were to successfully negotiate an end to the war and form an alliance with a rehabilitated Khieu Samphan, he would boost his chances of electoral victory, they said.
The Khmer Rouge, responsible for the death of more than one million Cambodians during their 1975-79 rule, was rocked by a violent split in its leadership last month.
Disagreement over whether to talk peace with the government is believed to have led to the split and the ouster of Pol Pot as supreme leader.
